value.overview: The Orange-breasted Falcon (Falco deiroleucus) is a scarce Neotropical raptor associated with mature tropical forests and rocky nesting sites. It is a compact, powerful falcon that hunts fast-flying birds and bats above the forest canopy. Although its geographic range extends from southern Mexico through much of South America, it is very unevenly distributed and poorly known in several regions. Central American populations are especially isolated and vulnerable, making this one of the least frequently encountered forest falcons.
value.classification: The Orange-breasted Falcon belongs to the family Falconidae, which includes falcons and caracaras. It is a member of the genus Falco and is closely associated in appearance with the Bat Falcon, although the two species differ in breast pattern, coloration, and range.
value.identification: Adults have a dark slate to blackish head and upperparts, a white throat, a strongly orange-rufous breast and belly, and dark barring or spotting on the lower body. The cere and legs are yellow to orange, and the bill is short and strongly hooked. In flight, it shows pointed wings and a relatively long tail. It can be confused with the Bat Falcon, but the Orange-breasted Falcon is generally larger and has a more extensively orange underbody. Juveniles are browner and less brightly colored.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges discontinuously from southern Mexico and Central America south through tropical South America to northern Argentina and Paraguay. In Costa Rica it is extraordinarily rare: historical specimens and older records document former occurrence, but extensive searches have found no established recent population, and it may be extirpated there. It is associated with lowland or lower-montane evergreen and semi-deciduous forest, especially large, relatively undisturbed forest landscapes containing tall emergent trees or large cliffs suitable for nesting.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident, with no regular long-distance migration known. In Costa Rica it should be regarded as a very rare or possibly extirpated former resident rather than a regular migrant; any modern occurrence would be exceptional and requires careful documentation.
value.breeding: In Mesoamerica, Orange-breasted Falcons usually nest on ledges or cavities on large cliffs surrounded by extensive forest. Nest sites may be reused, and pairs defend the surrounding area. Elsewhere in South America, they may also nest in large emergent trees. The species typically lays a small clutch, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Confirmed breeding in Mesoamerica is concentrated in Belize and Guatemala; no reliable recent breeding population is known from Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: Orange-breasted Falcons are aerial hunters that capture birds and bats, often pursuing prey above or along the forest canopy. They may also take large insects and other small vertebrates opportunistically. Their rapid, maneuverable flight allows them to attack fast-moving prey, and they commonly use exposed perches on cliffs or tall trees to watch for hunting opportunities. The species is one of the falcons most strongly associated with tropical forest environments.
value.behavior: This falcon is usually encountered singly or in pairs and is often inconspicuous until it makes a fast flight from a high perch. It spends considerable time watching from cliffs, dead branches, or emergent trees, then launches into rapid pursuit of prey. Pairs are territorial around nesting areas and may perform aerial displays. Because it is scarce, quiet when perched, and easily confused with the Bat Falcon, its distribution is probably under-recorded in some parts of its range.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although estimates remain uncertain because the species is rare, difficult to survey, and easily confused with the Bat Falcon. The Central American population has undergone a marked contraction and is now concentrated mainly in Belize and Guatemala, with isolated birds or small populations farther south.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include loss and fragmentation of mature tropical forest, reduction of suitable nesting cliffs and emergent trees, disturbance near nest sites, and the small size and isolation of remaining populations. In Costa Rica, the principal conservation issue is the apparent disappearance or extreme rarity of the species, which may reflect historical habitat change, low population density, and the difficulty of confirming records. Inadequate knowledge also limits effective protection.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect large tracts of mature forest and the cliffs, canyon walls, and emergent trees used for nesting. Prevent disturbance at suspected nest sites, retain forest corridors between protected areas, and support surveys using trained observers and photographic documentation. In Costa Rica, carefully verified sightings should be reported to national rare-bird authorities and conservation organizations, since reliable records could clarify whether a remnant population persists.
